questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Multiplicative Property
questions.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{1}{xy}\,\text{d}A$ over the rectangle $R=[1,e]\times [e,{e}^{2}].$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{xy}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x})\text{ }(\frac{1}{y})\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{e}^{{e}^{2}}\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡x]_{1}^{e}\cdot [\operatorname{ln}⁡y]_{e}^{{e}^{2}} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡e) \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (2-1) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{\sqrt{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\,{x}^{1/2}\,{y}^{1/2}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}})\text{ }(\sqrt{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral When the Integrand Contains Only One Variable
questions.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(3{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2})\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}3{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}6{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}3{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(2-0){\int }_{-1}^{0}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2({x}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{0}) \\  & =2({0}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}6{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(0-(-1)){\int }_{0}^{2}6{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{y}^{3}{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2\cdot {2}^{3}-0 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(3{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A=2+16=18.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{1+y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[1,2]\times [0,8].$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A & =(8-0){\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}{|}_{1}^{2}) \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{1}{8}-(-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(2-1){\int }_{0}^{8}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}{|}_{0}^{8} \\  & =\frac{{8}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2} \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}A=3+32=35.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{R}\frac{1+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[1,e]\times [0,\pi ].$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{1}{x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\text{ }\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1}{x}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(\pi -0){\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi \cdot [\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|]_{1}^{e} \\  & =\pi (\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(e-1){\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =(e-1)[-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(e-1)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =2(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{1+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{x}\,\text{d}A=\pi +2(e-1)=2e+\pi -2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate ${∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[-3,0]\times [0,4].$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(4-0){\int }_{-3}^{0}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]_{-3}^{0} \\  & =4(\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}-\frac{(-3)^{3}}{3}) \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(0-(-3)){\int }_{0}^{4}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =3[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{4} \\  & =3(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

The third integral is the double integral of unity:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\text{d}A=\text{Area}(R)=3\cdot 4=12\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A=36-24+12=24.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate ${∬}_{R}(2+2x-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A$,  where $R=[0,3]\times [0,2].$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(2+2x-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}2\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}2x\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is a constant, so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2\,\text{d}A=2\,\text{Area}(R)=2\cdot (3\cdot 2)=12.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The function under the second integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2x\,\text{d}A & =(2-0){\int }_{0}^{3}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot [{x}^{2}]_{0}^{3} \\  & =2({3}^{2}-(0)^{2}) \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the third integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}2y\,\text{d}A & =(3-0){\int }_{0}^{2}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =3\cdot [{y}^{3}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =3({2}^{3}-{0}^{3}) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}(2+2x-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A=12+18-24=6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Using Additivity of Double Integrals
questions.problem:
Given that $C$ and $D$ are finite, non-overlapping regions and that

$$
{∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=12,\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A=-8,
$$

find the value of 

$$
{∬}_{C\cup D}3f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the linearity and additivity of double integrals, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C\cup D}3f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A & =3{∬}_{C\cup D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A \\  & =3({∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A) \\  & =3(12-8) \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\, & \text{if}\,-1<x<1,\,0<y<\pi , \\ x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\, & \text{if}\,1<x<2,\,0<y<\pi ,\end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we have $R={R}_{1}\cup {R}_{2}$, where ${R}_{1}=(-1,1)\times (0,\pi )$ and ${R}_{2}=(1,2)\times (0,\pi ).$ So, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A= & ={∬}_{{R}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{R}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{{R}_{1}}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{R}_{2}}x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & =(1-(-1)){\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y+({\int }_{1}^{2}x\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y) \\  & =2[\operatorname{sin}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi }+[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]_{1}^{2}\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =2(0)+(2-\frac{1}{2})\cdot (-(-1)+1) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral Using the Multiplicative Property
canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} xy\ \!e^{x+y}\ \textrm d A$ over the rectangle $R= [0,1] \times [1,2].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We apply the multiplicative property of double integrals and then evaluate each of the integrals separately:

$$
\eqalign{
\iint\limits_{R}  xy\  e^{x+y}\: \textrm d A &= \iint\limits_{R} \Big( x\ \! e^x \Big)\Big( y\ \! e^{y} \Big) \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= \left(\int_0^1x\  e^{x}  \ \textrm d x\right)\left( \int_1^2 y \ \!e^{y} \ \textrm d y\right)\[5pt]
                                                                         &= \Big[x\ \!e^x-e^x\Big]_0^1 \cdot  \Big[y\ \!e^y-e^y\Big]_1^2\[5pt]
                                                                         &=  \Big(e^1-e^1 - \left(0-e^0\right)\Big) \cdot \Big(2e^2-e^2 - \left(e^1-e^1\right) \Big)\[5pt]
                                                                         &= 1\cdot e^2\[5pt]
                                                                         &= e^2
}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral When the Integrand Contains Only One Variable
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3)\text{ }\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}3\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's evaluate each of the three integrals.

- The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(4-2){\int }_{-1}^{3}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{-1}^{3} \\  & =2(\frac{27}{3}+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{56}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(3-(-1)){\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}y \\  & =4{\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}{|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{4}^{3}-\frac{4}{3}{2}^{3} \\  & =\frac{224}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The function under the third integral is a constant, so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}3\,\text{d}A=3\,\text{Area}(R)=3\cdot (2\cdot 4)=24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3)\,\text{d}A=\frac{56}{3}-\frac{224}{3}+24=-32.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Given that $C$ and $D$ are finite, non-overlapping regions and that

$$
\iint\limits_{C}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = 8,
\qquad
\iint\limits_{D}  f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A = -5,
$$

find the value of 

$$
\iint\limits_{C \cup D}  3f(x,y)\ \textrm{d}A.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the linearity and additivity of double integrals, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{C\cup D}3f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A & =3{∬}_{C\cup D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A \\  & =3({∬}_{C}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A) \\  & =3(8+(-5)) \\  & =3\cdot 3 \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A$, where

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14099811/assets/feda4016e31449244cf758fe239e49c6dd384a91b216763f72210b3c1b213827.png)
and  $R$ is the domain of $f.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that we have $R = R_1 \cup R_2,$ where $R_1= (0,2) \times (-1,0)$ and $R_2= (0,2) \times (0,1).$ So, we can write

$$
\eqalign{
\iint\limits_{R}  f(x,y)\ \textrm d A &= \iint\limits_{R_1} 2 \ \textrm d A + \iint\limits_{R_2}    \dfrac{1}{xy+x+y+1} \ \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= 2\iint\limits_{R_1} \textrm d A
+ \iint\limits_{R_2}  \dfrac{1}{(x+1)(y+1)} \ \textrm d A\[5pt]
&= 2(2-0)(0-(-1)) + \Bigg( \int_0^2 \dfrac{1}{x+1} \ \textrm d x \Bigg) \Bigg( \int_0^1 \dfrac{1}{y+1}\ \textrm d y \Bigg) \[5pt]
&= 4 + \Big[\ln(x+1)\Big]_0^2  \cdot \Big[\ln(y+1)\Big]_0^1\[5pt] 
&= 4+ \ln 3\ln 2.
}
$$
